- Reusable substrate: The kinetic theory / statistical-mechanics based equation of state for an ideal gas. In other words, a simple microscopic model of many noninteracting point particles in a container, whose collective behavior is captured by a macroscopic state equation relating pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of substance. The universal form PV = nRT (or PV = Nk_B T) embodies this substrate: a state relation tying macroscopic observables to the underlying microphysics (particle number, energy per degree of freedom, and momentum transfer).

- How each variable maps onto that abstract structure:
  - P (pressure): the macroscopic result of many molecular collisions with container walls. In kinetic theory, P is proportional to the momentum transfer rate to the walls, and for an ideal gas P ∝ (N/V) ⟨½ m v^2⟩. With equipartition ⟨½ m v^2⟩ = (3/2)k_B T, this becomes P = (N/V) k_B T, and hence PV = Nk_B T.
  - V (volume): the space available for particle motion; the container volume. Larger V reduces collision frequency and, all else equal, lowers pressure.
  - n (amount of substance): the amount of gas in moles. It scales the total number of particles, N = n N_A. The law PV = nRT shows how increasing the number of particles (at fixed P and T) requires more volume (or higher P or T to maintain the relation).
  - T (temperature): a measure of the average kinetic energy per degree of freedom of the molecules. In the kinetic theory / equipartition picture, temperature sets the energy scale of molecular motion: (1/2)m⟨v^2⟩ ∝ k_B T, and ⟨v^2⟩ ∝ T.
  - R (gas constant): the macroscopic constant that links microscopic constants to molar quantities. R = N_A k_B, so PV = nRT can be seen as PV = (N/V) (N_A k_B) T in particle terms, tying the microscopic energy–momentum picture to macroscopic, molar measurements.

- Extra note (why this is a reusable substrate): The ideal-gas state equation is a robust, widely applicable framework that arises from the same underlying microphysical assumptions (noninteracting particles, elastic collisions, equipartition). It can be extended or modified to relate other sets of intensive/extensive variables, but PV = nRT captures the core substrate that links microscopic motion to macroscopic observables.
